claim: Myosin motor domains perform an extraordinary diversity of biological functions despite sharing a common mechanochemical cycle.
source: Myosin motor domains perform an extraordinary diversity of biological functions despite sharing a common mechanochemical cycle.
evidence: This is a statement about myosin motor domains that is supported by established scientific knowledge about myosin function.

claim: Myosin-II motors power muscle contraction.
source: For example, myosin-II motors power muscle contraction, whereas myosin-V motors engage in intracellular transport.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about myosin-II function.

claim: Myosin-V motors engage in intracellular transport.
source: For example, myosin-II motors power muscle contraction, whereas myosin-V motors engage in intracellular transport.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about myosin-V function.

claim: Differences in myosins' tails and light chain-binding domains influence properties like localization and multimerization.
source: This diversity is in part due to differences in myosins' tails and light chain-binding domains, which influence properties like localization and multimerization (Krendel and Mooseker, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Krendel and Mooseker, 2005.

claim: Some of myosin functional diversity is encoded in the motor domains themselves.
source: However, some of this diversity is encoded in the motor domains themselves (Greenberg et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Greenberg et al., 2016.

claim: The speed of myosin movement along actin is set by the rate of ADP dissociation.
source: Similarly, the speed of myosin movement along actin (in the absence of opposing forces) is set by the rate of ADP dissociation (De La Cruz and Ostap, 2004), and it varies by four orders of magnitude from ~0.4 s−1 for non-muscle myosin-IIb (Nagy et al., 2013) to >2800 s−1 for myosin-XI (Ito et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to De La Cruz and Ostap, 2004, Nagy et al., 2013, and Ito et al., 2007.

claim: ADP release rate varies by four orders of magnitude from ~0.4 s−1 for non-muscle myosin-IIb to >2800 s−1 for myosin-XI.
source: Similarly, the speed of myosin movement along actin (in the absence of opposing forces) is set by the rate of ADP dissociation (De La Cruz and Ostap, 2004), and it varies by four orders of magnitude from ~0.4 s−1 for non-muscle myosin-IIb (Nagy et al., 2013) to >2800 s−1 for myosin-XI (Ito et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Nagy et al., 2013 and Ito et al., 2007.

claim: Myosin-Va is a high duty ratio motor.
source: Myosin-V family members contain both high duty ratio motors, like myosin-Va, (De La Cruz et al., 1999) and low duty ratio motors, like myosin-Vc (Takagi et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to De La Cruz et al., 1999.

claim: Myosin-Vc is a low duty ratio motor.
source: Myosin-V family members contain both high duty ratio motors, like myosin-Va, (De La Cruz et al., 1999) and low duty ratio motors, like myosin-Vc (Takagi et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Takagi et al., 2008.

claim: ADP release rates within the myosin-II family vary from ~0.4 s−1 (non-muscle myosin-IIb) to >400 s−1 (extraocular myosin-II).
source: Similarly, ADP release rates within the myosin-II family vary from ~0.4 s−1 (non-muscle myosin-IIb) (Nagy et al., 2013) to >400 s−1 (extraocular myosin-II) (Bloemink et al., 2013; Johnson et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Nagy et al., 2013, Bloemink et al., 2013, and Johnson et al., 2019.

claim: There is a correlation between the length of loop 1 and ADP release rates in myosin-II motors.
source: For instance, pioneering biochemical work Sweeney et al., 1998 demonstrated a correlation between the length of loop 1 and ADP release rates in myosin-II motors.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sweeney et al., 1998.

claim: An A223T mutation in human β-cardiac myosin causes a dilated cardiomyopathy.
source: For example, in human β-cardiac myosin, an A223T mutation causes a dilated cardiomyopathy (Ujfalusi et al., 2018) while an I263T mutation has the opposite effect, resulting in a hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (Tesson et al., 1998), despite being separated by less than 6 Å (Planelles-Herrero et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ujfalusi et al., 2018.

claim: An I263T mutation in human β-cardiac myosin results in a hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
source: For example, in human β-cardiac myosin, an A223T mutation causes a dilated cardiomyopathy (Ujfalusi et al., 2018) while an I263T mutation has the opposite effect, resulting in a hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (Tesson et al., 1998), despite being separated by less than 6 Å (Planelles-Herrero et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Tesson et al., 1998.

claim: The A223T and I263T mutations in human β-cardiac myosin are separated by less than 6 Å.
source: For example, in human β-cardiac myosin, an A223T mutation causes a dilated cardiomyopathy (Ujfalusi et al., 2018) while an I263T mutation has the opposite effect, resulting in a hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (Tesson et al., 1998), despite being separated by less than 6 Å (Planelles-Herrero et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Planelles-Herrero et al., 2017.

claim: The P-loop is a highly conserved structural element for nucleotide binding that is highly conserved across myosin motor domains.
source: Because of its high conservation, we reasoned that the P-loop would report on the conformation of the nucleotide binding site while still being comparable between motors with otherwise differing sequences.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the P-loop, also referenced by citation to Saraste et al., 1990 elsewhere in the text.

claim: Two milliseconds of all-atom, explicit-solvent molecular dynamics simulations were performed for twelve myosin motor domains.
source: To test this hypothesis, we ran an unprecedented two milliseconds of all-atom, explicit solvent molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of twelve myosin motors with diverse but well-established biochemical properties (Figure 1B, Tables 1, 2).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the simulations performed in this study.

claim: Crystal structures rarely sample P-loop conformations with RMSD >0.6 Å from the reference conformation.
source: We found very little structural diversity among crystal structures, which rarely sample any conformations with P-loop backbone RMSD >0.6 Å away (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Only 10 of 114 (9%) crystal structures' P-loop conformations were >0.6 Å RMSD from the reference conformation.
source: Only 10 of 114 (9%) crystal structures' conformations were >0.6 Å RMSD from the reference conformation, whereas fully 58% of the distribution observed in silico is above 0.6 Å RMSD from the reference conformation.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of crystal structure data and simulation data.

claim: 58% of the P-loop conformational distribution observed in silico is above 0.6 Å RMSD from the reference conformation.
source: Only 10 of 114 (9%) crystal structures' conformations were >0.6 Å RMSD from the reference conformation, whereas fully 58% of the distribution observed in silico is above 0.6 Å RMSD from the reference conformation.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of simulation data.

claim: Simulations of human β-cardiac myosin revealed extensive conformational heterogeneity in the P-loop.
source: In contrast to the relative uniformity among crystal structures, simulations revealed extensive conformational heterogeneity in the P-loop (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The lower basin in P-loop conformational space contains 91% of crystal structures (104/114).
source: The lower basin (<0.6 Å RMSD from the reference structure) contains 91% of crystal structures (104/114) and, because 80% (84/105) of these structures are bound to nucleotide, it is highly likely to represent a nucleotide-compatible conformation.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of crystal structure data.

claim: 80% (84/105) of crystal structures in the lower basin are bound to nucleotide.
source: The lower basin (<0.6 Å RMSD from the reference structure) contains 91% of crystal structures (104/114) and, because 80% (84/105) of these structures are bound to nucleotide, it is highly likely to represent a nucleotide-compatible conformation.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of crystal structure data.

claim: The lower basin likely represents a nucleotide-compatible conformation.
source: The lower basin (<0.6 Å RMSD from the reference structure) contains 91% of crystal structures (104/114) and, because 80% (84/105) of these structures are bound to nucleotide, it is highly likely to represent a nucleotide-compatible conformation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that most structures in the lower basin are nucleotide-bound.

claim: Regions outside the lower basin (≥0.6 Å RMSD) contain only 9% (10/114) of crystal structures.
source: In contrast, despite being populated roughly equally in simulation, regions outside the lower basin (≥0.6 Å RMSD) contain only 9% (10/114) of crystal structures.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of crystal structure data.

claim: Only one (11%) of the crystal structures outside the lower basin is nucleotide bound.
source: And, because only one (11%) of these structures is nucleotide bound, these regions are significantly depleted in nucleotide-bound structures (odds ratio = 0.03, p<1.3×10−5 by Fisher's exact test), strongly implying that they are less or not at all nucleotide compatible.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of crystal structure data.

claim: Regions outside the lower basin are significantly depleted in nucleotide-bound structures (odds ratio = 0.03, p<1.3×10−5 by Fisher's exact test).
source: And, because only one (11%) of these structures is nucleotide bound, these regions are significantly depleted in nucleotide-bound structures (odds ratio = 0.03, p<1.3×10−5 by Fisher's exact test), strongly implying that they are less or not at all nucleotide compatible.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of crystal structure data.

claim: Regions outside the lower basin are less or not at all nucleotide compatible.
source: And, because only one (11%) of these structures is nucleotide bound, these regions are significantly depleted in nucleotide-bound structures (odds ratio = 0.03, p<1.3×10−5 by Fisher's exact test), strongly implying that they are less or not at all nucleotide compatible.
evidence: This is an inference based on the statistical analysis showing depletion of nucleotide-bound structures.

claim: The most probable single P-loop state is the A state (49%).
source: The most probable single state is the A state (49%), which encompasses the entire lower basin and, as we will see below, appears to form favorable interactions with nucleotide based on the conformation of the P-loop.
evidence: This claim is supported by MSM analysis of simulation data.

claim: The excited, apparently nucleotide-disfavoring conformations in the upper basin are split into 3 states, B-D, which together account for 50% of the equilibrium probability.
source: The excited, apparently nucleotide-disfavoring conformations in the upper basin are split into 3 states, B-D, which together account for 50% of the equilibrium probability.
evidence: This claim is supported by MSM analysis of simulation data.

claim: β-cardiac myosin spends about equal time in nucleotide-favorable (state A) and nucleotide-unfavorable states (states B-D) in simulations.
source: Thus, β-cardiac myosin spends about equal time in nucleotide-favorable (state A) and nucleotide-unfavorable states (states B-D) in simulations.
evidence: This claim is supported by MSM analysis of simulation data.

claim: The dominant geometrical difference between nucleotide-favorable and nucleotide-unfavorable P-loop states is the orientation of the peptide bond between S180 and G181.
source: Comparing the states of our MSM reveals that the dominant geometrical difference between nucleotide-favorable and nucleotide-unfavorable P-loop states is the orientation of the peptide bond between S180 and G181 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of MSM states shown in Figure 3C.

claim: In the nucleotide-favorable state A, the S180 backbone carbonyl is oriented away from the phosphates of the nucleotide.
source: In the nucleotide-favorable state A (Figure 3D, lower right inset), the S180 backbone carbonyl (shown in pink sticks with a white arrow) is oriented away from the phosphates of the nucleotide, enabling the nucleotide to bind to the active site.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: In nucleotide-disfavoring states (B-D), the S180 backbone carbonyl is oriented toward the phosphate groups of the nucleotide.
source: In contrast, nucleotide-disfavoring states (labeled B-D in Figure 3D) orient the S180 backbone carbonyl toward the phosphate groups of the nucleotide.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: High duty ratio motors have a stronger in silico preference for nucleotide-favoring P-loop states than low duty ratio motors.
source: As expected, high duty ratio motors have a stronger in silico preference for nucleotide-favoring P-loop states than low duty ratio motors (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Of 29 unliganded crystal structures, 8/20 (40%) of low duty ratio motors' P-loops crystallized outside the A state, whereas 0/9 (0%) high duty ratio motors' P-loops crystallized outside state A (p<0.034 by Fisher's exact test).
source: Of 29 unliganded crystal structures, 8/20 (40%) of low duty ratio motors' P-loops crystallized outside the A state, whereas 0/9 (0%) high duty ratio motors' P-loops crystallized outside state A (p<0.034 by Fisher's exact test, see Materials and methods).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of crystal structure data.

claim: There is a strong correlation between motors' duty ratios and their preferences for the nucleotide-favorable A state over the nucleotide-unfavorable B state.
source: As expected, we find a strong correlation between motors' duty ratios and their preferences for the nucleotide-favorable A state over the nucleotide-unfavorable B state (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: High duty ratio motors have a strong preference for the A state (negative free energy difference).
source: Specifically, high duty ratio motors have a strong preference for the A state (negative free energy difference) while low duty ratio motors spend more time in state B (positive free energy difference).
evidence: This claim is supported by MSM analysis of simulation data.

claim: Low duty ratio motors spend more time in state B (positive free energy difference).
source: Specifically, high duty ratio motors have a strong preference for the A state (negative free energy difference) while low duty ratio motors spend more time in state B (positive free energy difference).
evidence: This claim is supported by MSM analysis of simulation data.

claim: There is a strong positive relationship (Pearson's R = 0.99) between the P(A→B) fit by MSMs and in vitro ADP release rate for the Sweeney dataset.
source: As expected, there is a strong positive relationship (Pearson's R = 0.99) between the P(A→B) fit by our MSMs and in vitro ADP release rate (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The correlation between P(A→B) and ADP release rate (Pearson's R = 0.99) is stronger than the equivalent correlation for the length-based model (Pearson's R = 0.72).
source: This is stronger than the equivalent correlation for the length-based model (Pearson's R = 0.72).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of correlation coefficients.

claim: Despite diverse experimental conditions, there is a reasonable correlation between P(A→B) and ADP release across all data sets (Pearson's R = 0.75).
source: Consistent with our expectations, and despite the diverse experimental conditions, we still observe a reasonable correlation between P(A→B) and ADP release across all data sets (Figure 5E, Pearson's R = 0.75).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The P(A→B) correlation with ADP release (Pearson's R = 0.75) dramatically improves on the length-based model (Pearson's R = 0.14).
source: This dramatically improves on the length-based model (Pearson's R = 0.14).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of correlation coefficients.

claim: In MYO6, the A state of the P-loop is stabilized by an interaction between the backbone carbonyl oxygen of the P-loop serine (homologous to S180 in MYH7) and the sidechain amide group of the switch-II residue K670.
source: First, we observed that the A state of the P-loop in the high duty ratio motor MYO6 is stabilized by an interaction between the backbone carbonyl oxygen of the P-loop serine (homologous to S180 in MYH7) and the sidechain amide group of the switch-II residue K670 (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Low duty ratio myosin-II motors (MYH13, MYH7, and MYH10) feature an isoleucine at the position homologous to K670 in MYO6.
source: A notable difference occurs in the low duty ratio myosin-II motors in our study (MYH13, MYH7, and MYH10), all of which feature an isoleucine at this position (MYH7 I674).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis.

claim: The sidechain of I674 in MYH7 almost never forms a direct interaction (distance <0.35 nm) with S180 even in P-loop state A.
source: Figure 6B shows that the sidechain of I674 in MYH7 almost never forms a direct interaction (distance <0.35 nm) with S180 even in P-loop state A, whereas K670 of MYO6 almost always does when the P-loop occupies the A state.
evidence: This claim is supported by distance analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: K670 of MYO6 almost always forms a direct interaction with the P-loop serine when the P-loop occupies the A state.
source: Figure 6B shows that the sidechain of I674 in MYH7 almost never forms a direct interaction (distance <0.35 nm) with S180 even in P-loop state A, whereas K670 of MYO6 almost always does when the P-loop occupies the A state.
evidence: This claim is supported by distance analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The B state of the P-loop in the low duty ratio motor MYH7 is stabilized by an interaction between the backbone carbonyl oxygen of S242 (in the Switch-I loop) and the S180 sidechain hydroxyl group.
source: Second, we also observed that the B state of the P-loop in the low duty ratio motor MYH7 is stabilized by an interaction between the backbone carbonyl oxygen of S242 (in the Switch-I loop) and the S180 sidechain hydroxyl group (Figure 6C), but that this interaction does not occur in the high duty ratio motor MYO7A (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The interaction between S242 and S180 does not occur in the high duty ratio motor MYO7A.
source: Second, we also observed that the B state of the P-loop in the low duty ratio motor MYH7 is stabilized by an interaction between the backbone carbonyl oxygen of S242 (in the Switch-I loop) and the S180 sidechain hydroxyl group (Figure 6C), but that this interaction does not occur in the high duty ratio motor MYO7A (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The duty ratio and the rate of ADP release are not captured by a single structural element, but rather by the distribution of conformations that the motor explores in solution.
source: Our studies demonstrate that the duty ratio and the rate of ADP release are not captured by a single structural element, but rather by the distribution of conformations that the motor explores in solution.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation and analysis results presented in the study.

claim: The distribution of P-loop conformations is sensitive to relevant sequence changes, both large and small, throughout the myosin motor domain.
source: Throughout our simulations, we observed that the distribution of P-loop conformations is sensitive to relevant sequence changes, both large and small, throughout the myosin motor domain.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results.

claim: Capturing the difference between the wild-type and alanine-substituted chicken gizzard myosins required the model to capture the allosteric perturbation induced by a change of a few dozen atoms in a molecule of ~12,500 atoms at a distance of ~25 Å.
source: Thus, capturing the difference between the wild-type and alanine-substituted chicken gizzard myosins (Figure 5C), for instance, required the model to capture the allosteric perturbation induced by a change of a few dozen atoms in a molecule of ~12,500 atoms at a distance of ~25 Å (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is an inference about what the model captured based on the simulation results.

claim: The excited states of the P-loop observed in silico may be related to the biochemically-observed 'open' and 'closed' states that nucleotide-free myosin motors populate in vitro.
source: One tantalizing interpretation of the excited states of the P-loop we observe in silico is that they may be related to the biochemically-observed 'open' and 'closed' states that nucleotide-free myosin motors populate in vitro (Geeves et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the simulation results, supported by citation to Geeves et al., 2000.

claim: The equilibrium between nucleotide-favorable and nucleotide-disfavorable conformations predicted duty ratio.
source: Similarly, we showed that the equilibrium between nucleotide-favorable and nucleotide-disfavorable conformations predicted duty ratio, while the rate of transition predicted ADP release rate.
evidence: This is a summary of the results presented in the study.

claim: The rate of transition between nucleotide-favorable and nucleotide-disfavorable conformations predicted ADP release rate.
source: Similarly, we showed that the equilibrium between nucleotide-favorable and nucleotide-disfavorable conformations predicted duty ratio, while the rate of transition predicted ADP release rate.
evidence: This is a summary of the results presented in the study.

claim: Simulations only require a reasonable homology model as a starting point.
source: Importantly, our simulations only require a reasonable homology model as a starting point, so our methods should be applicable to a broad range of motor variants, including mutations implicated in disease.
evidence: This is a statement about the methodology used in the study.

claim: The methods should be applicable to a broad range of motor variants, including mutations implicated in disease.
source: Importantly, our simulations only require a reasonable homology model as a starting point, so our methods should be applicable to a broad range of motor variants, including mutations implicated in disease.

claim: The ability of the isolated motor domain's fluctuations to predict biochemical parameters likely stems from a link between the isolated and bound conformational distributions.
source: The ability of the isolated motor domain's fluctuations to predict these parameters likely stems from a link between the isolated and bound conformational distributions.
evidence: This is an inference about the mechanism underlying the predictive power of the simulations.

claim: The motor domain active site must adopt certain key conformations during its functional interactions with binding partners (i.e. nucleotide and actin).
source: In other words, because the motor domain active site must adopt certain key conformations during its functional interactions with binding partners (i.e. nucleotide and actin), it is nearly guaranteed to at least transiently sample those conformations even in the absence of those binding partners.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on protein dynamics principles.

claim: The motor domain is nearly guaranteed to at least transiently sample key conformations even in the absence of binding partners.

evidence: This is a logical inference based on protein dynamics principles.

claim: The P-loop (or Walker A motif) is a common structural element for nucleotide binding that is highly conserved across myosin motor domains.
source: Indeed, our simulations reveal a surprising degree of conformational heterogeneity, particularly in the highly conserved P-loop (or Walker A motif), a common structural element for nucleotide binding that is highly conserved across myosin motor domains (Saraste et al., 1990).

claim: Simulations reveal a surprising degree of conformational heterogeneity in the P-loop.
source: Indeed, our simulations reveal a surprising degree of conformational heterogeneity, particularly in the highly conserved P-loop (or Walker A motif), a common structural element for nucleotide binding that is highly conserved across myosin motor domains (Saraste et al., 1990).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results.

claim: Sequences produce distinct biochemical phenotypes by modulating the relative probabilities of an ensemble of conformations primed for different functional roles.
source: We hypothesized that sequences produce distinct biochemical phenotypes by modulating the relative probabilities of an ensemble of conformations primed for different functional roles.

claim: Comparing motors reveals shifts in the balance between nucleotide-favorable and nucleotide-unfavorable P-loop conformations that predict experimentally measured duty ratios and ADP release rates better than sequence or individual structures.
source: Comparing motors reveals shifts in the balance between nucleotide-favorable and nucleotide-unfavorable P-loop conformations that predict experimentally measured duty ratios and ADP release rates better than sequence or individual structures.

claim: Protein dynamics encode function.
source: This hypothesis was inspired by a growing body of work showing that protein dynamics encode function (Henzler-Wildman and Kern, 2007; Knoverek et al., 2019), even in the absence of relevant binding partners (Bowman and Geissler, 2012; Hart et al., 2016; Porter et al., 2019a).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Protein dynamics encode function even in the absence of relevant binding partners.
source: This hypothesis was inspired by a growing body of work showing that protein dynamics encode function (Henzler-Wildman and Kern, 2007; Knoverek et al., 2019), even in the absence of relevant binding partners (Bowman and Geissler, 2012; Hart et al., 2016; Porter et al., 2019a).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: As sequence changes modulate motors' preferences for different states of the mechanochemical cycle, they likely also have a systematic effect on the distribution of conformations explored by the motor, even in the absence of binding partners.
source: In the case of myosin, we reasoned that as sequence changes modulate motors' preferences for different states of the mechanochemical cycle, they likely also have a systematic effect on the distribution of conformations explored by the motor, even in the absence of binding partners.
evidence: This is a logical inference that forms part of the study's hypothesis.

claim: Comparing the distribution of conformations that isolated motor domains sample in solution should reveal signatures of their biochemical differences.
source: Therefore, comparing the distribution of conformations that isolated motor domains sample in solution should reveal signatures of their biochemical differences.

claim: Motors that prefer nucleotide-favorable P-loop conformations in isolation pay a lower energetic cost to adopting these same nucleotide-favorable conformations when they form a complex with nucleotide.

claim: A large free energy difference between ADP-bound and nucleotide-free states is associated with a low duty ratio.
source: Supporting this logic, it has been observed that, absent load, a large free energy difference between ADP-bound and nucleotide-free states is associated with a low duty ratio (Bloemink and Geeves, 2011; Nyitrai and Geeves, 2004).

claim: A preference for the nucleotide-favorable A state should correlate with low duty ratio.

claim: MD and MSMs constitute a powerful platform for identifying relationships between the sequence of individual motor domains and their mechanochemical cycles.

claim: The structures of motor domains with vastly different biochemical properties are often nearly indistinguishable.

source: It also orients the negative end of the carbonyl bond's electric dipole toward the nucleotide binding site and the negatively charged phosphates of ADP and ATP.

claim: The observations about the geometry of the excited, nucleotide-disfavoring state in the upper basin are consistent with a lowered capacity for nucleotide binding.

source: The low duty ratio motor explores both upper and lower basins (Figure 4A, left) while the high duty ratio motor strongly prefers the lower basin (Figure 4A, right).

claim: The myosin with wild-type loop 1 had an ADP release rate more than three times faster than predicted by the length-based model.
source: A notable exception, however, was the myosin with wild-type loop 1, which had an ADP release rate more than three times faster than predicted by the length-based model (Figure 5B).

source: This deviation from a purely length-driven ADP release rate led these authors to hypothesize that there must also be sequence-specific effects of loop 1 on ADP release rate.
evidence: This is a statement about the hypothesis of previous work.

evidence: This is a statement about previous work.

claim: The rank order of the four isoforms' ADP release rates is correct when using P(A→B) from MSMs.

evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparison of model predictions to experimental data.

claim: The sequence change between wild type and the alanine mutant is small (only five residues differ).
source: Together, the fact that the sequence change is small (only five residues differ between wild type and the alanine mutant) and the change is distant (~25 Å) from the P-loop indicate that our model is exquisitely sensitive to sequence, even at sites distant from the active site.
evidence: This is a statement about the sequence differences between constructs.

claim: The model is exquisitely sensitive to sequence, even at sites distant from the active site.

claim: MYH7 and MYH13 have roughly the same loop 1 length but their ADP release rates differ by about an order of magnitude (59 s−1 vs 400 s−1).
source: These motor domains are an interesting case because, at 80% sequence identity, their sequences differ much more than Sweeney et al's constructs, and these differences are distributed throughout the protein. Crucially, and despite having roughly the same loop 1 length, their ADP release rates differ by about an order of magnitude (59 s−1 vs 400 s−1).
evidence: This is a statement about the biochemical properties of these motors.

claim: MYH7 and MYH13 have 80% sequence identity.
source: These motor domains are an interesting case because, at 80% sequence identity, their sequences differ much more than Sweeney et al's constructs, and these differences are distributed throughout the protein.
evidence: This is a statement about the sequence similarity between these motors.

claim: Motors' properties are very sensitive to magnesium, temperature, and light chain identity.
source: Owing to the fact that Johnson et al's data were collected under different experimental conditions than Sweeny et al's data (5 mM MgCl2 at 25°C vs 1 mM MgCl2 at 20°C with different light chains), we only expect a general trend to hold, since motors' properties are very sensitive to magnesium, temperature, and light chain identity (Chizhov et al., 2013; Heissler and Sellers, 2014; Lewis et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Under the matched experimental conditions for MYH7 and MYH13, the model finds the correct order of ADP release rates.
source: Importantly, under the matched experimental conditions for MYH7 and MYH13 we still find the correct order of ADP release rates (Figure 3C, yellow points), suggesting that this method generalizes well to the larger phylogenic distances between myosin isoforms.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparison of model predictions to experimental data.

claim: MYO1B and MYH10 are correctly identified as very slow releasers of ADP.
source: Furthermore, MYO1B and MYH10 are correctly identified as very slow releasers of ADP, although the point estimates appear to be quite noisy.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparison of model predictions to experimental data.

claim: MYH10 is known to be exquisitely sensitive to light chains.
source: MYH10 is known to be exquisitely sensitive to light chains (Heissler and Sellers, 2014), so it is not surprising that it is one of the greatest outliers given that we did not include these in our simulations.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citation to Heissler and Sellers, 2014.

claim: The sequences of motors' P-loops are identical.
source: Even though the sequences of motors' P-loops are identical, their conformational distributions differ.
evidence: This is an observation about sequence conservation.

source: This suggests that interactions with other structural elements in the motor domain bias the P-loop's conformational distribution and our that models capture these effects.

source: This suggests that interactions with other structural elements in the motor domain bias the P-loop's conformational distribution and our that models capture these effects.
evidence: This is an inference based on the model's predictive power.

claim: The substitution of an aliphatic residue at the position homologous to K670 in myosin-II motors destabilizes the nucleotide-favoring A state.
source: We propose that the substitution of an aliphatic residue at this position in myosin-II motors destabilizes the nucleotide-favoring A state, leading to an increased preference for the nucleotide-disfavoring B state, ultimately resulting in a lower predicted duty ratio.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on structural analysis.

claim: Many other low duty ratio myosin classes, such as MYO1B, feature a lysine at the position homologous to K670 in MYO6.
source: Notably, however, many other low duty ratio myosin classes, such as MYO1B which we simulated here and correctly identify as a low duty ratio motor, feature a lysine at this position, implying that this substitution may be a peculiar innovation limited to myosin-IIs.
evidence: This is an observation about sequence variation across myosin classes.

claim: The substitution of an aliphatic residue at the position homologous to K670 may be a peculiar innovation limited to myosin-IIs.
source: Notably, however, many other low duty ratio myosin classes, such as MYO1B which we simulated here and correctly identify as a low duty ratio motor, feature a lysine at this position, implying that this substitution may be a peculiar innovation limited to myosin-IIs.
evidence: This is a speculation based on sequence analysis.

claim: The interaction between S242 and S180 in MYH7 is specific to the nucleotide-disfavoring B state.
source: This interaction is specific to the nucleotide-disfavoring B state of MYH7 (Figure 6D), and hence presumably stabilizes that P-loop state in MYH7 relative to MYO7A.
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The interaction between S242 and S180 in MYH7 requires the Switch-I loop to move 'inwards,' toward the peptide bond between G464 and A463.
source: As shown in Figure 6C, this interaction in MYH7 requires the Switch-I loop to move 'inwards,' toward the peptide bond between G464 and A463, with which it also sometimes interacts.
evidence: This is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: At the position homologous to A463 in MYH7, the high duty ratio motor MYO7A features a phenylalanine (F439).
source: At the position homologous to A463, however, the high duty ratio motor MYO7A features a phenylalanine (F439).
evidence: This is a statement about sequence differences.

claim: The bulky, aromatic sidechain in MYO7A (F439) prevents the Switch-I loop from engaging the P-loop serine's sidechain, whereas the small aliphatic one (MYH7's A463) does not.
source: We propose that the bulky, aromatic sidechain in MYO7A (F439) prevents the Switch-I loop from engaging the P-loop serine's sidechain, whereas the small aliphatic one (MYH7's A463) does not.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on structural analysis.

claim: The bulky aromatic sidechain in MYO7A leads to a lower overall preference for the nucleotide-disfavoring B state and thus a higher overall duty ratio prediction.
source: On net, this leads to a lower overall preference for the nucleotide-disfavoring B state in MYO7A and thus a higher overall duty ratio prediction.
evidence: This is an inference based on the proposed mechanism.

claim: MYO6 has an alanine at the position homologous to A463 in MYH7.
source: Interestingly, MYO6 has an alanine at this position, indicating that this substitution is not strictly required for high duty ratio.
evidence: This is a statement about sequence variation.

claim: The substitution at position 463 is not strictly required for high duty ratio.
source: Interestingly, MYO6 has an alanine at this position, indicating that this substitution is not strictly required for high duty ratio.

claim: Physically realistic, atomically detailed models can provide mechanistic insight into how sequence variation modulates specific interactions to alter a protein's function.
source: These examples demonstrate how physically realistic, atomically detailed models can provide mechanistic insight into how sequence variation modulates specific interactions to alter a protein's function.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the structural analysis examples.

claim: There are many interactions at play, and consideration of multiple interactions is necessary to fully explain duty ratio.
source: Of course, there are many interactions at play, and consideration of multiple interactions is necessary to fully explain duty ratio.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the complexity of the system.

claim: A successful pipeline for predicting duty ratio predictions will probably require additional molecular dynamics simulations for any new variant.
source: Therefore, a successful pipeline for predicting duty ratio predictions will probably require additional molecular dynamics simulations for any new variant.
evidence: This is a speculation about future applications of the method.

claim: A fruitful design strategy would be to select mutations based on structural logic, then to simulate the newly designed sequences to check that they behave as intended (in silico), and then to perform experimental tests of these predictions.
source: Specifically, we suggest that a fruitful design strategy would be to select mutations based on logic like that outlined above, then to simulate the newly designed sequences to check that they behave as intended (in silico), and then to perform experimental tests of these predictions.
evidence: This is a proposed strategy for future work.

source: Such an approach has proved powerful in past applications to other proteins (Hart et al., 2016; Zimmerman et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Hart et al., 2016 and Zimmerman et al., 2017.

claim: Computer simulations of isolated myosin motor domains were used to predict the in vitro ADP release rate and duty ratio of unloaded myosin motors.
source: In this work, we used computer simulations of isolated myosin motor domains to predict the in vitro ADP release rate and duty ratio of unloaded myosin motors.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's approach.

claim: Systematic shifts in the distribution of conformations that a motor explores correlate with changes in biochemistry.
source: To do this, we identified systematic shifts in the distribution of conformations that a motor explores that correlate with changes in biochemistry, rather than by directly simulating the biochemical processes themselves, which would have been prohibitively expensive.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's approach.

claim: Binding partners (actin and nucleotide) and structural elements outside the motor domain almost certainly affect the distribution of conformations.
source: While binding partners (actin and nucleotide, for instance) and structural elements outside the motor domain almost certainly affect the distribution of conformations, our results demonstrate that it is nevertheless possible to extract reasonable estimates for at least some unloaded biochemical properties from only the isolated motor domain's conformational distribution.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of limitations and a statement about the results.

claim: It is possible to extract reasonable estimates for at least some unloaded biochemical properties from only the isolated motor domain's conformational distribution.

claim: The techniques presented here are expected to be of use for any protein where the physics that maps sequence to biochemistry is not straightforward.
source: Finally, because we find no reason to believe our approach's applicability is limited to myosin motors, we expect the techniques we have presented here to be of use for any protein where the physics that maps sequence to biochemistry is not straightforward.
evidence: This is a speculation about the broader applicability of the methods.
